title: 2 Samuel 9:1–8
context: With his kingdom established, David asks whether anyone remains of Saul’s house to whom he can show kindness for Jonathan’s sake, keeping the covenant he made with his friend (1 Samuel 20:14–17, 42). Ziba, a former servant of Saul, tells him of Jonathan’s son Mephibosheth, lame in both feet since childhood (2 Samuel 4:4), living in the house of Machir at Lo Debar. David brings him to court, tells him not to fear, restores Saul’s land to him, and promises him a permanent place at the king’s table. Mephibosheth responds by calling himself a dead dog.

verses.text: David said, “Is there yet any who is left of Saul’s house, that I may show him kindness for Jonathan’s sake?”
verses.arminianNotes: David seeks anyone left of Saul’s house to show kindness for Jonathan’s sake. Arminian readers see David freely keeping his sworn word to Jonathan (1 Samuel 20:14–17), seeking out an opportunity rather than waiting for one.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see covenant faithfulness, hesed, in David’s initiative, which many read as a picture of God’s own covenant love. Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as loyalty to a promise, shown toward a family that could have been treated as rivals.

verses.text: There was of Saul’s house a servant whose name was Ziba, and they called him to David; and the king said to him, “Are you Ziba?” He said, “I am your servant.”
verses.arminianNotes: Ziba, a servant of Saul’s house, is called before the king. Arminian readers note that David uses ordinary inquiry to find Jonathan’s family, relying on someone who knew the old royal household well.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that Ziba will reappear in later chapters with a more complicated role (16:1–4; 19:24–30). Both traditions read his introduction here simply as the means by which David learns where Mephibosheth is living.

verses.text: The king said, “Is there not yet any of Saul’s house, that I may show the kindness of God to him?” Ziba said to the king, “Jonathan still has a son, who is lame in his feet.”
verses.arminianNotes: David asks whether anyone remains to whom he may show “the kindness of God.” Arminian readers see David modeling his kindness on God’s, offering it freely to someone who has no claim on him.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the phrase as pointing beyond David to the steadfast love of God, which David’s kindness reflects. Shared ground: Ziba mentions the son’s lameness, and both traditions note that David’s kindness is not conditioned on usefulness.

verses.text: The king said to him, “Where is he?” Ziba said to the king, “Behold, he is in the house of Machir the son of Ammiel, in Lo Debar.”
verses.arminianNotes: Ziba says Jonathan’s son is in the house of Machir son of Ammiel in Lo Debar. Arminian readers note that he seems to be living quietly away from the court, east of the Jordan, perhaps out of caution.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that Machir later helps David when he flees Absalom (17:27–29). Both traditions acknowledge that Lo Debar’s exact location is uncertain, though it is generally placed in Gilead, east of the Jordan.

verses.text: Then King David sent and brought him out of the house of Machir the son of Ammiel, from Lo Debar.
verses.arminianNotes: David sends and brings him from Machir’s house in Lo Debar. Arminian readers note that the king takes the initiative to bring Mephibosheth to court, rather than waiting for him to come seeking favor on his own.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see in the king’s summons a picture many apply to grace that seeks out the one who could not come by himself. Shared ground: both traditions draw this application as an illustration, not as the main point of the historical account.

verses.text: Mephibosheth, the son of Jonathan, the son of Saul, came to David, fell on his face, and showed respect. David said, “Mephibosheth?” He answered, “Behold, your servant!”
verses.arminianNotes: Mephibosheth falls on his face before David and calls himself his servant. Arminian readers note his fear, since a new king often removed members of the former dynasty, and Mephibosheth may expect the worst.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see humility before the king, as the grandson of Saul bows before the man God chose in Saul’s place. Both traditions read the scene as tense, with Mephibosheth unsure of what David intends to do with him.

verses.text: David said to him, “Don’t be afraid, for I will surely show you kindness for Jonathan your father’s sake, and will restore to you all the land of Saul your father. You will eat bread at my table continually.”
verses.arminianNotes: David tells him not to fear, restores Saul’s land, and promises a place at his table continually. Arminian readers see generous kindness that goes beyond what Mephibosheth could expect or request.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see David acting on his covenant with Jonathan, giving honor to the son for the father’s sake. Shared ground: both traditions read the promise of land and a seat at the table as an extraordinary act of covenant kindness.

verses.text: He bowed down, and said, “What is your servant, that you should look at such a dead dog as I am?”
verses.arminianNotes: Mephibosheth calls himself a dead dog unworthy of the king’s notice. Arminian readers see deep humility, perhaps shaped by years of living in obscurity as a disabled member of a fallen royal family.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see a recognition of unworthiness that many apply to how people receive grace from God. Both traditions note that “dead dog” was a strong expression of self-abasement in that culture, used elsewhere in Samuel (1 Samuel 24:14).
